lines.note: Hashigaki denotes writing in a margin. The further explanation concerns a letter's added writing, not necessarily a modern book preface.

runs.text: Præcipuè, o que ſe torna a eſcreuer no principio

lines.note: Latin praecipue means especially. The definition singles out material written again at the beginning of a letter, continuing below.

runs.text: da carta em letra mais miuda.

lines.note: The added text uses smaller handwriting. This physical description is important: hashigaki here is not limited to a formal introductory essay.
Hashigawarake is an earthenware dish associated with chopsticks. The concave basin or lid-like form is explicit in the Portuguese.

runs.text: barro em que ſe leuão os dous paozinhos com

lines.note: The two little sticks are carried in the earthenware vessel. The middle of paozinhos is worn, so the existing spelling is retained provisionally.
The sticks used for eating are placed inside the dish. Metidos refers to the sticks, not to the people eating.

runs.text: Paos como frechais da ponte ſobre

lines.note: Hashigeta denotes bridge timbers, compared with frechais or structural beams. The next row specifies what rests on them.
The balusters rest on these timbers. This closes the bridge construction definition, not the ladder entry below.
Hashigo or hashinoko here names the transverse sticks of a portable ladder. The narrower rung sense is explicit, despite modern hashigo commonly denoting the whole ladder.
Completes escada de mão, a portable ladder. The final label is visibly X., not OCR A.; it is a usage mark rather than Japanese a.

runs.text: O eſtar a hũa parte, ou canto da ca-

lines.note: Hashii is sitting or remaining at a side or corner. The printed j represents the final i; the interior hyphen is not a line-break marker.
The possible location is a house or veranda. The final P. is visibly slanted and belongs to the usage notation, not the Japanese expression.

runs.text: Faxin. Fariuo toru. i, Monouo nù.

lines.note: Hashin, taking up the needle, is explained as sewing something. Monouo nù represents mono wo nuu; the unusual accent is retained, not converted from modern kana expectations.
Hashin wo suru means sewing with a needle. Portuguese aguha is the printed historical form and is not expanded to agulha.
Completes fazer custura, doing needlework. Custura's vowel differs from modern costura but is retained diplomatically.
Hashinja denotes a tailor or seamstress. The -ja element supplies the person associated with the sewing activity defined above.
Hashi no ko again denotes ladder rungs. This spaced phrase is preserved independently of the joined faxinoco spelling above.
Hashikin is described as a kind of senkō, thin incense sticks. Tagui means a kind or class; the printed Xencono is not expanded to a guessed long-vowel spelling.
Delgados specifies that the incense sticks are slender. It is a physical-line continuation, not an isolated gloss for hashira.
Hashira means a wooden post or column. Esteo is a supporting post, agreeing with colunna rather than referring to a personal name.
Hashirakashi is causative, making someone run. The listed -su and -aita endings belong to the older conjugational notation.
The running may be a rapid errand with a message. Recado provides a practical example of the causative action, not a separate lexical sense.

runs.text: O aleuantar as colunas de pao

lines.note: Hashiradate is raising wooden building posts. The noun combines hashira and tate, with voiced d in the compound.

runs.text: no lugar do edificio, ou caſas. Vt,

lines.note: The posts are raised on the building site. The final Faxira- begins the Japanese example continued below.
Completes hashiradate wo suru, performing the raising of posts. This short row belongs to the preceding example and is not a new headword.
Hashiragakushi is an ornament or painting used to conceal a post. Guernição is retained as the printed Portuguese variant.

runs.text: que ſe dependura na colunna pera a encobrir,

lines.note: The covering hangs on the column to conceal it. The Portuguese object refers back to the column, matching Japanese kakushi 'hiding'.
Adds the purpose of ornamentation as well as concealment. This is the end of the hashiragakushi definition.

runs.text: Pao que ſe prèga ao comprido na

lines.note: Hashirayose is a strip of wood nailed lengthwise. Pregar here means fastening with nails, not preaching.

runs.text: ombreira da porta peraque entre a porta, & a

lines.note: The strip is on a door jamb so that the door and jamb meet without a gap. The printed peraque remains joined.

runs.text: ombreira não fique eſpaço aberto pera poder

lines.note: The purpose is to prevent an open space between jamb and door. The negative não is essential to the construction's function.

runs.text: ver, ou meter os dẽdos. No Cami ſe diz.

lines.note: No gap should permit looking or inserting fingers. Cami names the upper-region dialect; its local typeface is italic in this occurrence.
Toyose is the regional alternative just introduced. It is a continuation of the previous definition, not a new alphabetically placed headword.
This hashiri is a throwing cane or dart. The Portuguese distinguishes it from the running verb and kitchen fixture below.
Hashiri wo tsukiidasu means throwing or thrusting out the canes. The Portuguese arremesar supports the projectile interpretation.

runs.text: Lugar como taboa onde lauão a louça

lines.note: A different hashiri is a board-like kitchen washing place. The definition concerns crockery, not an act of running.

runs.text: na cozinha, & per onde eſcorre a agoa.

lines.note: Water drains from this kitchen washing surface. The drainage explains the functional relationship to flowing or running water.
Hashiri is the running verb; the added Fugir introduces fleeing. The scan reads Fugir, without the extra i inserted by OCR.

runs.text: do ſeruiço do ſenhor, acolherſe da guerra, &c.

lines.note: The fleeing is from a lord's service or from war. Acolher-se here participates in a withdrawal sense, not merely welcoming someone.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Ir a Fune à vela. Vt,

lines.note: Another sense concerns a boat travelling under sail. Fune is embedded Japanese within italic Portuguese; the final Funega begins the example.
Fune ga hashiru completes the sailing example. Uma ga hashitta is then explicitly translated as the horse died, a special usage rather than literal running.
Caualo completes the horse-death expression. Item introduces things jumping or bursting in fire, again an extended use of hashiru.

runs.text: tourar algũà couſa no fogo. Vt,

lines.note: Shio ga hashiru is the salt example, supported by Portuguese sal below. OCR Xiurga cannot parse; the worn final vowel of Xiuo and following ga are recoverable from the scan.

runs.text: O ſal dentro do fogo ſalta. ¶

lines.note: The salt jumps in the fire. The final Cu- begins kuri, chestnuts, on the next physical line.
Kuri ga hashiru describes chestnuts bursting. The Portuguese translation parallels the salt example rather than assigning hashiru a new unrelated headword.
The chestnuts burst in fire, followed by usage label X. Chi ga hashiru then introduces blood spurting; the scan supports g rather than OCR j.
Blood spurts, then katana ga hashiru introduces a sword example continued in the other column. The damaged n letters caused OCR Cataliaga; the sword translation confirms Katana.
The sword comes out of its sheath by itself, completing katana ga hashiru from the previous column. Catana is italic here; X. is a Roman usage label.
Cami is split across rows and names the region using sayabashiru. The alternative verb appears italic here, while Chiye no begins a new Japanese example.
Chie no hashitta mono ja describes an astute person. Portuguese sagaz agrees with intellectual quickness, not the literal running of wisdom.
Hashiru uma ni muchi is the proverb about whipping a running horse. Prou. is an editorial label, not part of the Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Ao que tem inclinação, & impeto pera

lines.note: The proverb concerns someone already inclined and eager to act. This qualification is necessary to understand the horse comparison.

runs.text: fazer algũa couſa exhortalo, he como dar

lines.note: Exhorting such a person is like urging on the running horse. The scan reads exhortalo, not OCR exhertalo; the meaning and visible o agree.

runs.text: com a vara no caualo, que vai correndo.

lines.note: The comparison concludes with striking a horse that is already running. It is a proverb explanation, not a recommendation inserted by the transcriber.
Hashiriagari means running upward. The past ending is atta, supported by the scan and NINJAL, not OCR aeta.
Hashirikakari means charging at a run. Correndo has a worn e but is a single Portuguese word, not the OCR gap corr ndo.
Hashirikaeri means returning at a run. The cayeri spelling and etta ending correspond to kaeri/kaetta.
Hashirichiri means running while scattering. Chiru supplies dispersal, consistent with espalhando-se.
Hashiri kogura is illustrated with wo suru. NINJAL also records cogura, so it is not normalized to an anticipated kurabe; Vt is the italic example label.

runs.text: Correrem dous a par, ou muitos juntos.

lines.note: The explanation is two running abreast or many together. This supports a collective-running sense without requiring a modern race-word substitution.
Hashirikorobi means falling while running. The contracted ôda ending is preserved rather than expanded to modern koronda.
Hashirikoye means running over something. Koye represents koe, crossing over, and the object continues across the Portuguese word break.
Completes dalgũa couſa correndo, running over some thing. The contracted nasal remains within the physical continuation.
Hashiri kudari means running down. The printed internal space is retained, unlike neighboring joined compounds.
Hashirikusa denotes a spreading skin complaint in this historical definition. The contemporary disease comparison is recorded as the dictionary's description, not a modern diagnosis.

runs.text: bretoeja que ſe eſpalha, & dilata pello corpo

lines.note: The rash spreads over the body. The printed bretoeja is preserved rather than modernized to brotoeja.
Muito perigosa completes the dictionary's characterization of the complaint as dangerous. It modifies the preceding illness description.
Hashiri ide is running out. The printed j in jde represents vowel i, supported by NINJAL, rather than a Japanese consonantal j.
Hashiri jidameki describes running with considerable bustle. The gi spelling represents ji and agrees with the agitation described below.
Rebuliço or pressa specifies commotion or haste. The short continuation completes the preceding verb's definition.
Hashirimai names a great lord's trusted attendant. Privado is a favored confidential servant here, not the adjective 'private'.

runs.text: que tudo faz, & a tudo acode com preſteza.

lines.note: The attendant does everything and responds promptly. This functional explanation accounts for the running-about component of the Japanese noun.
The verb hashirimai means serving promptly. Its inflections distinguish it from the uninflected attendant noun above.
Hashirimawari is running around. Mawari supplies the circular movement independently of the running prefix.
Hashirimeguri has the same meaning as hashirimawari, as Idem states. The unusual abbreviated utta ending is also in NINJAL and remains unchanged.
Hashirimodori means returning at a run. The damaged d is supported by the Portuguese tornar and the headword data.

runs.text: O que fugio do ſeruiço do ſenhor.

lines.note: Hashirimono is someone who fled a lord's service. This noun uses the fugitive sense of hashiru established in the other column.
Hashirimukai means running to face or confront someone. The Portuguese de fronte continues below.
Fronte completes the facing position. It belongs to hashirimukai, not to the next running-ahead verb.
Hashirinobi means running ahead. The listed ita ending is retained as printed and supported by NINJAL despite nearby alternative nobi conjugations.
Completes passar a diante, passing ahead. Both Portuguese formulations explain the same Japanese compound.
Hashiritobi wo suru is making a running jump. Vt is italic, and the scan contracts the final Portuguese Corren- to Corrẽ-.
Completes correndo saltar, jumping with a run-up. This is the end of the noun-plus-suru example.
The separately conjugated hashiritobi verb has the same running-jump sense. Its ǒda past ending is not normalized to modern tonda.
Hashiriyagura is an uncovered defensive platform or bastion. Yagura supplies the structural noun, rather than a verb of running.
The structure lacks a roof or awning. Tellado is the retained printed spelling, not silently corrected to telhado.
Hashiriyori means approaching at a run. Yoru supplies approach, agreeing with chegar-se.

runs.text: Reſto que fica da conta, ou numero im-

lines.note: Hashita denotes a remainder or incomplete quantity. Im- continues into imperfeito below; its terminal division mark is visible at the rule.

runs.text: perfeito, & falto daquelle que he ordinario,

lines.note: The amount falls short of the ordinary full quantity. This is a numerical sense, not the later social-status use of hashita.

runs.text: como ſe faltaſſem 10. ou 20. folhas de pa-

lines.note: The example is ten or twenty paper sheets short of a hundred. The printed figures are quantities and retain their following punctuation.

runs.text: pel pera cento que tem hua mão de

lines.note: A full unit of torinoko paper is described here as one hundred sheets. Torinoco is Roman within the Portuguese explanation, and the scan ends this row with a colon.

runs.text: aquelle numero imperfeito, & falto ſe dirà

lines.note: The incomplete quantity is said to be the following Japanese expression. The scan supports dirà rather than the OCR divided diri-.
Issoku no hashita means the incomplete remainder of a bundle or counted unit. It completes the numerical example rather than beginning a new entry.
The cross-reference reads Faxit. mono, pointing toward the following hashitamono entry. OCR Eixit does not match the surviving capital and following letters.
